section_summary: This section follows the Allied occupation’s effort to dissolve Japan’s zaibatsu and other concentrations of economic power. State and Army Department papers debate compensation, appeals, the scope of deconcentration, and its effect on economic recovery, while press reports and diplomatic correspondence track the program’s reception. The section ends in the middle of a research report comparing Japanese legislation with FEC-230.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transferring responsibilities for designated zaibatsu families
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Transfers Ministry of Finance functions concerning designated zaibatsu families to the Holding Company Liquidation Commission.
subfiles.summary: Directs transfer of powers, records and related information to the commission.

subfiles.title: Letter sending the Zaibatsu Mission Report to Kenneth Colegrove
subfiles.about: Sends the mission report and press release while explaining that its recommendations remain classified.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the proposed deconcentration program has yet to be considered by the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Letter thanking Carson Purcell for Raymond Vernon’s mission service
subfiles.about: Thanks the Securities and Exchange Commission for assigning Raymond Vernon to the zaibatsu mission.
subfiles.summary: Praises Vernon’s work and cites Marquat’s approval of the mission.

subfiles.title: Letter thanking Oscar Ryder for Benjamin B. Wallace’s mission service
subfiles.about: Thanks the Tariff Commission for assigning Benjamin B. Wallace to the zaibatsu mission.
subfiles.summary: Praises Wallace’s service and the mission’s contribution to policy on Japanese combines.

subfiles.title: Deconcentration of Economic Power in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Army concern, press criticism and efforts to revise deconcentration policy.
subfiles.summary: Describes FEC-230’s origins, unauthorized disclosure and criticism, and a proposed State–Army substitute.

subfiles.title: British parliamentary questions on dissolution of Japanese holding companies
subfiles.about: Reports House of Commons questions about sales of assets by Japan’s Holding Company Liquidation Commission.
subfiles.summary: The British reply describes holdings already taken over and planned limits on purchases by individuals and firms.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting a Central News Agency article
subfiles.about: Transmits an article criticizing the occupation’s treatment of the zaibatsu.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the article was widely published in China.

subfiles.title: Backbone of Zaibatsu Control Said Still Intact
subfiles.about: Argues that zaibatsu influence persists through banks, subsidiaries and former associates.
subfiles.summary: Calls for stronger measures to prevent former zaibatsu interests from regaining control.

subfiles.title: Chinese statement on subsidies to state enterprises
subfiles.about: Relays a Chinese government statement on reducing subsidies to state enterprises.
subfiles.summary: Says some enterprises, especially in communications, will remain partly subsidized.

subfiles.title: Letter to Edward C. Welsh on foreign investments in zaibatsu firms
subfiles.about: Asks whether Washington should address a reported policy gap concerning foreign investors in the zaibatsu split-up.
subfiles.summary: Quotes a New York Times report and seeks clarification of SCAP’s wishes.

subfiles.title: Japanese Deconcentration Ordinance and SWNCC 302/2
subfiles.about: Records a State–Army discussion of objections to the proposed deconcentration ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Lists concerns about compensation, firm size, patents, judicial review and the commission’s discretion. State and Army agree to examine a revised ordinance promptly.

subfiles.title: Possible Queries Regarding FEC 230
subfiles.about: Suggests replies to anticipated Army questions on compensation and labor organizations.
subfiles.summary: Defends limited compensation and explains why unions were exempted from Japanese antitrust restrictions.

subfiles.title: Statement of U.S. Policy Toward Economic Recovery of Japan
subfiles.about: Sets economic recovery and a self-supporting Japanese economy as urgent occupation priorities.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the occupation’s political and security achievements against the Basic Post-Surrender Policy. It argues that Japan’s economic weakness requires continued American support, then calls for a shift in emphasis toward recovery, trade and reduced dependence on U.S. resources.

subfiles.title: Conversation with John J. McCloy on reconsidering the Zaibatsu Program
subfiles.about: Records McCloy’s views on reviewing zaibatsu policy and its implementation.
subfiles.summary: McCloy recalls high-level approval of the basic deconcentration directive and warns that reversing it would disrupt the occupation. He distinguishes that settled policy from the ordinance’s detailed procedures, which he says responsible officials can review without convening an outside panel.

subfiles.title: Developments in proposed reconsideration of the Zaibatsu Program
subfiles.about: Reports discussions between Royall and Lovett over a joint statement and revisions to zaibatsu policy papers.
subfiles.summary: Lovett seeks specific Army objections before revising the ordinance and asks that McCloy’s views be shared with Gray.

subfiles.title: Draft letter to Kenneth C. Royall on reviewing the Zaibatsu Program
subfiles.about: Addresses a proposed comprehensive review of the zaibatsu program.
subfiles.summary: The heavily degraded text concerns the scope and timing of a policy review.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on dissolution of economic power in Japan
subfiles.about: Outlines the zaibatsu program and the State Department’s position amid Army objections.
subfiles.summary: Traces the program from the 1945 occupation directives through holding-company liquidation and proposed legislation. It argues that limited compensation is inherent in reducing former owners’ power and that delay could hinder recovery. It also addresses fears that the program is un-American or excessive.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Lovett on eliminating excessive concentrations
subfiles.about: Recommends a State Department response to the Army’s proposed cable on Japan’s deconcentration ordinance.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum accepts several Army suggestions on wording, industry standards and appeals. It opposes proposals that would weaken the ordinance or decide broader policy questions before review, and recommends sending State’s alternative cable and commentary to Royall.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Royall on the proposed cable to MacArthur
subfiles.about: Offers an alternative cable and asks for specific Army objections to broader policy.
subfiles.summary: Seeks immediate guidance for MacArthur while reserving wider policy questions for review.

subfiles.title: Draft cable permitting passage of the deconcentration bill with changes
subfiles.about: Lists amendments under which Washington would cease objecting to the deconcentration bill.
subfiles.summary: Proposes clarifying excessive concentrations, requiring supporting data, lengthening appeal periods and setting standards by industry.

subfiles.title: Commentary on proposed Army cable and State revisions
subfiles.about: Explains State’s changes to the Army’s proposed instructions on Japan’s deconcentration ordinance.
subfiles.summary: State rejects language prejudging the broader policy review and argues against making dissolution merely permissive. It discusses price influence, appeals, judicial review and compensation, distinguishing corporate reorganization from seizure of family assets. It also opposes Washington review of each industry standard as an unnecessary delay and intrusion on SCAP’s implementation authority.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting a Times editorial on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, United States Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Transmits a Times editorial on dissolving the zaibatsu.
subfiles.summary: Highlights the editorial’s warning that restoring zaibatsu power would strengthen Japan’s old political forces.

subfiles.title: Struggle in Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses doubts about MacArthur’s zaibatsu policy and the political cost of relaxing it.
subfiles.summary: Argues that restoring zaibatsu leaders could endanger democratic gains despite immediate economic pressures.

subfiles.title: Zaibatsu Program: Newsweek inquiry
subfiles.about: Records discussions with a Newsweek representative about State–Army disagreements and the Japanese deconcentration law.
subfiles.summary: Wisner recounts an inquiry prompted by cables about delaying and then permitting the law. He says State and Army are jointly reviewing the program and cautions against describing their cable as a compromise between opposing policies. The memorandum also records competing background accounts and Wisner’s reason for speaking with the reporter.

subfiles.title: Letter to Royall on revisions to SWNCC 302/2
subfiles.about: Responds to Army proposals for revising deconcentration policy and sending a reviewer to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Suggests a conference could settle most remaining differences and promises a separate reply on the proposed mission.

subfiles.title: Royall letter proposing a senior review mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Sends Army objections and a proposed rewrite of SWNCC 302/2, and proposes a senior mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Royall argues that reviewers on the ground should assess the occupation’s economic direction promptly.

subfiles.title: Army request for a State economist in General Draper’s party
subfiles.about: Explains the decision on Army’s request to include a State Department economist in Draper’s Japan mission.
subfiles.summary: Wisner traces the mission’s origins and names its proposed civilian participants. Lovett declines to assign a State representative and instead arranges consultations with Kennan in Japan, preserving State’s ability to assess the mission’s recommendations after its return.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the General Contractors’ Association
subfiles.about: Transmits a press release announcing the association’s designation as a closed institution.
subfiles.summary: Says dissolution should allow democratic construction trade associations to develop.

subfiles.title: General Contractors’ Association to Be Designated Closed Institution
subfiles.about: Explains why the former construction control association will be closed by March 1948.
subfiles.summary: SCAP cites continued wartime control practices and personnel, and supports new democratic trade associations. Page 117 also contains an unrelated brief item about a Bronze Star presentation.

subfiles.title: Review of Zaibatsu Policy Paper—SWNCC 302/2
subfiles.about: Compares Army and State working revisions of the deconcentration policy paper.
subfiles.summary: Says remaining differences appear resolvable and points to State’s added section on economic recovery.

subfiles.title: Implementation of FEC-230 in Japan
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Office of Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a study of implementation and consistency of Japanese deconcentration laws with FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: Finds substantial legal preparation but major unfinished tasks, including securities liquidation and credit reform.

subfiles.title: Transmission of OIR 4602 (PV)
subfiles.from: Division of Research for Far East
subfiles.about: Transmits a preliminary report on Japanese actions implementing FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: Notes the appended list of laws and a related Far Eastern Commission synopsis.

subfiles.title: Japanese Legislation and Actions Implementing FEC-230
subfiles.from: Division of Research for Far East, Office of Intelligence Research
subfiles.about: Compares Japanese deconcentration legislation and administrative action with successive provisions of FEC-230.
subfiles.summary: The preliminary report examines definitions, dissolution standards, holding-company liquidation, interlocking directors, contracts, patents and personnel restrictions. It finds some measures implemented and others incomplete or less stringent than FEC-230. Its discussion of compensation and securities sales notes uncertainty over whether former zaibatsu owners could regain power. The report continues beyond page 127.
